newsitem.title: USA: N. Carolina Assembly eyes education, Medicaid.
newsitem.headline: N. Carolina Assembly eyes education, Medicaid.

text.p: North Carolina General Assembly formally opens its legislative session Wednesday with education, Medicaid reform and establishment of a state lottery expected to dominate their agenda.
Most of Wednesday's session was expected to be devoted to administrative matters and the selection of leaders.

Gov Jim Hunt is scheduled to release his budget proposal for 1997-98 and 1998-99 in two or three weeks. But the governor has already said he will ask lawmakers to cut state programs by $250 million this year and $150 million a year for the next four years to free up additional funds for education.
The $250 million figure represents about 2.5 percent of the state's $10 billion annual budget.

The Democratic governor said the cuts, combined with rising tax revenue, would allow the state to raise teachers salaries to the national average by 2000 and expand the Smart Start preschool program to all 100 counties.
State economists have said they expect General Fund revenue growth to slow to 5 or 6 percent, down from 8 percent in the late 1980s.
Voters approved $1.8 billion in school bonds in November, which will add annual debt service payments of $181 million a year by 2000.
But the News & Record newspaper quoted Hunt Wednesday as saying he has no intention of lowering his goals for education.
"I'm not asking us for something that will take an extraordinary effort forever. I'm asking for four years -- four years to get North Carolina's schools where they ought to be," he told the paper.
Hunt did not specify what cuts he would seek, but said some savings could be achieved by using managed care to slow growth in Medicaid spending.
Under an amendment approved by voters in November, the governor has veto powers for the first time.
Rep. Toby Fitch, D-Wilson, has also said he will re-introduce a bill calling for establishment of a state lottery.

Similar bills have failed in recent years, but polls suggest growing support. A poll conducted earlier this month for the Charlotte News & Observer and television station WCNC showed 62 percent of respondents favor a lottery and 83 percent believe legislators should let voters decide the issue.
